title: The ten-day retreat, going home
hook: the hardest part: carrying the calm into ordinary life

segments.voice: Yesterday, metta day: a last sit of loving-kindness, then silence lifts and the dining hall roars. Your line was metta day. Whom did you wish well before you spoke? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

The envelope comes back. Inside, the phone, and when it wakes up it starts buzzing and doesn't stop: messages, alerts, a calendar full of next week. The drive home has traffic. The grocery store on the way is louder than you remember, and brighter. Someone cuts in line, and something old and hot rises in the chest, right on schedule. On the last morning of the retreat, the calm felt solid enough to stand on. By dinner, it's thinner. Teachers of these retreats often say this is where the real work starts. Today: the ten-day retreat, going home.
screen: `THE PHONE STARTS BUZZING.` → `SOMEONE CUTS IN LINE.` → `THE CALM GROWS THIN.`

segments.voice: First, the thinning. The calm of a retreat was made in special conditions: silence, bells, no choices. Out here, the conditions are gone, and the calm fades. Teachers say that is normal, and that the calm was never really the point. The point was learning to see the mind, and that can come home. Second, an old Zen picture of it. The ox-herding pictures are a series of Zen images. A herder searches for a lost ox, a picture of the mind, finds its tracks, catches it, tames it, rides it home. Then herder and ox both vanish, into an empty circle. The series doesn't stop there. In its last picture, the herder walks into the town marketplace, barefoot, belly round, hands open, mixing with ordinary people. The verse with it says he has no need of special powers; the withered trees bloom wherever he goes. The path doesn't end on the mountain. It ends in the market. Third, one habit. Teachers on retreat courses encourage students to keep some practice at home: a sit in the morning or evening, a pause before eating, a day of silence now and then. Some students go home vowing to keep everything and keep nothing. One habit, kept, carries further. Fourth, the test. The person who cuts in line, the coworker, the family at the dinner table, is where the practice now lives. The retreat was not an escape from ordinary life. It was training for it. The ten-day retreat ends the moment you drive away, and then, slowly, it begins again.
screen: `THE CALM GROWS THIN.` · `THE OX-HERDER REACHES THE MARKET.` · `ONE HABIT, KEPT.` · `THE PRACTICE LIVES AT HOME NOW.` · then, large: `HANDS OPEN, IN THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to try it, if you'd like. Sit and breathe. Then choose one retreat habit you could keep, small enough to do even on a bad day. Maybe a few breaths before you look at your phone in the morning. Maybe a pause before meals. Maybe a short sit at night. Pick just one. See yourself doing it tomorrow, in your actual kitchen, on your actual morning. Then let the choice rest, and come back to the breath, the way you would on a retreat. The bell holds the time.
The ten-day retreat. Its last lesson comes after it ends: carrying what was learned in silence back into traffic, kitchens and crowded rooms. Today's word.
Your line: carry it home. Today, do the one habit you chose, once, in the most ordinary place you'll be. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: After a meditation retreat, Buddhist teachers commonly encourage students to keep a regular practice at home, such as a daily sit, and to bring the retreat's attention into work, family and ordinary errands.

pairs: small enough for a bad day

myth: if the calm fades after a retreat, the retreat failed
teachers say fading is normal; the calm was made in special conditions.
the ox-herding pictures end on a mountaintop
the last picture shows the herder walking into the marketplace, hands open.
retreats are meant as training for ordinary life
the practice now lives at home, in traffic and at the dinner table.

fork.setup: you're home from a retreat, full of resolve. what do you take on?
options: keep every part of the retreat schedule at once.
keep one small habit you can do even on a bad day.
wait until the next retreat to practice again.
fork.reveal: teachers encourage some practice at home. one habit, kept, carries further than many dropped.

original.note: Pali bhavana: cultivation, bringing into being; the word often used for meditation as an ongoing practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: a retreat gives you a calm that lasts.
what it means: the calm thins once you're home; the work is carrying what you learned into ordinary life.
what a scholar hears: the ox-herding pictures' last scene: the herder in the marketplace, hands open, where the withered trees bloom.

sources.ref: The ox-herding pictures (Kuoan Shiyuan's verses), final picture

notes: Ox-herding pictures (Kuoan/Kakuan series) paraphrased: search, tracks, catching, taming, riding home, both forgotten (empty circle), and the final 'entering the marketplace with helping hands'; the verse's 'no need of magic powers... withered trees bloom' is paraphrased. Confirm sequence summary and paraphrase.
The outline's 'the hardest part' is attributed to teachers ('often say this is where the real work starts'). Confirm.
'Teachers on retreat courses encourage students to keep some practice at home': general; confirm.
Original: bhavana (भावना) as cultivation / meditation practice; confirm.
Editor: the tenth picture does not follow the empty circle directly (a 'return to the source' comes between); reworded 'and then, in the last picture'.
